title: Products and Quotients of Functions
overview: Revenue is price **times** attendance. Food per person is food **divided by** population. A swinging pendulum is a wave **times** a decaying exponential. In this section you will multiply and divide functions, find holes and asymptotes, predict symmetry, and model real situations with products and quotients.
objectives: Determine equations for $f(x)g(x)$ and $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ and sketch their graphs.
Determine the domain and range of products and quotients, identifying holes and asymptotes.
Predict and prove the symmetry (even/odd) of products and quotients.
Explain why multiplication of functions is commutative but division is not.
Model damped oscillations as a sinusoid times an exponential.
Solve problems involving revenue, per-capita amounts and probabilities.

lessons.title: Products of Functions
lessons.body:
> A combined function of the form $y = f(x)g(x)$ is the **product** of $f$ and $g$: multiply the outputs at each $x$. Notation: $(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)$.

Unlike sums, there is no simple "stacking" picture for products – but your polynomial and factoring skills make products easy to analyse.

### Example
Let $f(x) = x + 3$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 8x + 15$.

$$y = f(x)g(x) = (x+3)(x^2 + 8x + 15) = x^3 + 11x^2 + 39x + 45$$

To sketch it, **factor** instead of expanding:

$$y = (x+3)(x+3)(x+5) = (x+3)^2(x+5)$$

* zeros: $-3$ (order 2 – the graph touches the x-axis and turns) and $-5$ (order 1 – it crosses)
* y-intercept: 45 (constant term)
* leading coefficient positive, degree 3 → falls to the left, rises to the right
* domain and range: $\mathbb{R}$

```plot
title: y = (x + 3)²(x + 5)
f: (x+3)^2*(x+5)
domain: -7, 1
range: -10, 50
points: (-3,0), (-5,0), (0,45)
ticks: 1, 10
```

### Quick sign facts for a product
* $f(x)g(x) = 0$ wherever **either** factor is zero.
* $f(x)g(x) > 0$ where both have the same sign; $< 0$ where they have opposite signs.
* Where one factor is a "slowly changing" positive function (like $0.95^x$), it **scales** the other factor.

lessons.title: Quotients of Functions: Holes and Asymptotes
lessons.body:
> A combined function $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ is the **quotient** of $f$ and $g$, defined only where $g(x) \ne 0$.

**Domain rule:** the domain of $f/g$ is the domain common to $f$ and $g$, **with all zeros of $g$ removed**.

### Example
With $f(x) = x + 3$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 8x + 15$:

$$\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{x+3}{(x+3)(x+5)} = \frac{1}{x+5}, \quad x \ne -3, -5$$

Always find the domain from the **original** (unsimplified) form:

| What happens at the excluded value | Feature of the graph |
|---|---|
| factor **cancels** ($x = -3$) | a **hole** at $(-3, \tfrac{1}{-3+5}) = (-3, \tfrac12)$ |
| factor **remains** in the denominator ($x = -5$) | a **vertical asymptote** $x = -5$ |

The graph is $y = \frac1x$ translated 5 units left, with a hole at $(-3, \tfrac12)$. Horizontal asymptote $y = 0$, so the range is $\{y \in \mathbb{R}, y \ne 0, y \ne \tfrac12\}$.

```plot
title: y = (x+3)/((x+3)(x+5)) – hole at (−3, ½)
f: 1/(x+5)
domain: -10, 2
range: -4, 4
asymptote x: -5
asymptote y: 0
points: (-3,0.5)
```

### Order matters
$\dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)}$ is the **reciprocal** of $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, a different function: here $\dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)} = x + 5$, $x \ne -3$ – a line with a hole. Multiplication of functions is commutative ($fg = gf$); division is not.

lessons.title: Symmetry of Products and Quotients
lessons.body:
Recall: $f$ is **even** if $f(-x) = f(x)$ (symmetric about the y-axis) and **odd** if $f(-x) = -f(x)$ (point symmetry about the origin).

| Even functions | Odd functions |
|---|---|
| $x^2,\ x^4,\ \cos x,\ |x|$ | $x,\ x^3,\ \sin x,\ \tan x$ |

The symmetry of a product (or quotient) follows the same pattern as multiplying signs:

| Factors | Product / quotient | Like… |
|---|---|---|
| even × even | **even** | (+)(+) = + |
| odd × odd | **even** | (−)(−) = + |
| even × odd | **odd** | (+)(−) = − |

**Proof (even × odd).** Let $f$ be even and $g$ odd, $h(x) = f(x)g(x)$. Then
$$h(-x) = f(-x)g(-x) = f(x)[-g(x)] = -h(x),$$
so $h$ is odd. The other cases are proved the same way, and quotients behave identically (as long as you exclude the zeros of the denominator).

**Examples:** $x^2\cos x$ is even; $x\sin x$ is even; $x^3\cos x$ is odd; $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is odd ÷ even = odd. ✓

lessons.title: Damped Oscillations: Sinusoid × Exponential
lessons.body:
A swing after one push, a released pendulum, or a plucked guitar string all move back and forth with **decreasing amplitude**. This is **damped harmonic motion**, modelled by a product:

$$y(t) = \underbrace{A\cos(kt)}_{\text{periodic part}} \times \underbrace{b^t}_{\text{decay, } 0<b<1}$$

* The trig factor makes it oscillate; its period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$.
* The exponential factor shrinks the amplitude. The curves $y = \pm A b^t$ form an **envelope** that the graph bounces between.
* At $t = 0$: $y = A$ – the starting displacement.

```plot
title: x(t) = 10cos(2t)(0.95)^t with envelope ±10(0.95)^t
f: 10*cos(2*x)*0.95^x | label=x(t)
f: 10*0.95^x | dashed; label=envelope
f: -10*0.95^x | dashed
domain: 0, 30
range: -11, 11
ticks: 5, 5
```

**When has the amplitude halved?** Solve $b^t = 0.5$: $t = \dfrac{\log 0.5}{\log b}$. For $b = 0.95$: $t \approx 13.5$ s.

**Effects of changing the model:**
* Less air resistance → $b$ closer to 1 → slower decay.
* Longer pendulum → slower swing → longer period → smaller $k$.

lessons.title: Applications: Revenue, Per-Capita Rates and Probability
lessons.body:
Many quantities are naturally **products** or **quotients** of other quantities.

| Quantity | Combination |
|---|---|
| Revenue | price × number sold, $R = P \cdot N$ |
| Food per person (per capita) | food ÷ population, $\dfrac{F}{P}$ |
| Probability of a prize | prizes ÷ people, $\dfrac{C}{N}$ |
| "Both events happen" probability | $p_1 \times p_2$ |

### Baseball marketing
Ticket price drops as games are played: $P(g) = 25 - 0.1g$ dollars. Attendance (hundreds) rises: $N(g) = 10 + 0.2g$.

Revenue (hundreds of dollars):
$$R(g) = (25 - 0.1g)(10 + 0.2g) = -0.02g^2 + 4g + 250$$
a parabola opening down with vertex at $g = \dfrac{-4}{2(-0.02)} = 100$. Revenue grows until game 100, then falls – the strategy works only in the short term.

Free caps given (hundreds): $C(g) = 2 - 0.04g$. The chance a fan gets a cap is
$$p(g) = \frac{2 - 0.04g}{10 + 0.2g}, \qquad p(5) = \frac{1.8}{11} \approx 0.16 \;(16\%).$$

### Comparing growth and decline
A quotient $\dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)} > 1$ means "more than enough" (surplus), $< 1$ means "not enough" (shortage), and $= 1$ marks the **crisis point** where they are equal.

keyTerms.definition: $(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)$; domain is the common domain of $f$ and $g$.
$\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, defined on the common domain with the zeros of $g$ removed.
A single missing point in a graph, occurring where a factor cancels from the numerator and denominator.
$f(-x) = f(x)$ for all $x$; the graph has line symmetry about the y-axis.
$f(-x) = -f(x)$ for all $x$; the graph has point symmetry about the origin.
Cyclic motion whose amplitude decreases over time, modelled by a sinusoidal function multiplied by a decaying exponential.

workedExamples.problem: Ticket price $P(g) = 25 - 0.1g$ dollars, attendance $N(g) = 10 + 0.2g$ hundred fans. Model revenue and decide whether the plan increases revenue.
steps: Revenue increases until game 100, then decreases. Only $g \ge 0$ has meaning.
workedExamples.answer: Revenue rises in the short term, peaking at game 100, then falls.

workedExamples.title: Proving a symmetry rule
workedExamples.problem: Prove that the product of two odd functions is even, and classify $y = x\sin x$.
steps: $x$ and $\sin x$ are both odd, so $x\sin x$ is even – its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
workedExamples.answer: odd × odd = even; $x\sin x$ is even.

misconceptions.myth: The domain of $\dfrac{f}{g}$ can be read from the simplified form.
misconceptions.fact: Use the **original** form. A factor that cancels still makes the function undefined there – it leaves a hole.
They are reciprocals. Division is not commutative.

misconceptions.myth: The product of two odd functions is odd.

misconceptions.fact: 10 is only the starting amplitude. The amplitude at time $t$ is $10(0.95)^t$.

misconceptions.myth: A hole and a vertical asymptote are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: A hole is one missing point (factor cancels); an asymptote is where the function grows without bound (factor stays in the denominator).

realWorld.title: Ticket pricing
realWorld.body: Lowering the price brings in more fans, but revenue = price × attendance can still fall. Writing revenue as a product reveals the best game (or price) for maximum revenue.

realWorld.title: Per-capita food supply
realWorld.body: Economists compare food production to population with the quotient $F/P$. A value above 1 is a surplus; below 1 is a shortage.

realWorld.title: Shock absorbers and swings
realWorld.body: Car suspensions are designed so bumps produce damped oscillations that die out quickly – a sinusoid multiplied by a fast-decaying exponential.

realWorld.title: Chance of a prize
realWorld.body: A probability is a quotient: favourable outcomes ÷ possible outcomes, e.g. caps given away ÷ fans attending.

practice.question: Let $f(x) = x + 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 4$. Find $y = f(x)g(x)$ and state its domain and range.
practice.hint: Expand; the result is a cubic.

practice.question: For the same functions, state the domain of $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ and of $\dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)}$.
practice.solution: $x^2 + 4 > 0$ always, so $\dfrac{f}{g}$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$ (no asymptotes). $\dfrac{g}{f}$ needs $x \ne -2$: vertical asymptote $x = -2$.

practice.question: Classify $y = x^2\sin x$ as even, odd or neither.
practice.solution: $x^2$ even, $\sin x$ odd → odd. Check: $(-x)^2\sin(-x) = -x^2\sin x$.

practice.question: Let $f(x) = x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 5x + 6$. Simplify $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ and describe its graph.
$x(t) = 8\cos(\pi t)(0.9)^t$. Find the period and the time for the amplitude to fall to 4.
Explain why $\tan x$ is odd using the symmetry of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
With $P(g) = 25 - 0.1g$ and $N(g) = 10 + 0.2g$, compute the revenue at game 20.

summary: $(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)$ and $\left(\frac fg\right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$; the domain is the common domain, minus zeros of the denominator.
Find holes and asymptotes from the **unsimplified** quotient: cancelled factor → hole; remaining factor → vertical asymptote.
Symmetry: even·even = even, odd·odd = even, even·odd = odd (same for quotients).
Multiplication of functions is commutative; division is not ($g/f$ is the reciprocal of $f/g$).
A sinusoid times a decaying exponential models damped harmonic motion; the exponential forms the envelope.
Products model revenue and joint probability; quotients model per-capita amounts and probabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine an equation for $y = f(x)g(x)$ in factored and expanded form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the key features needed to sketch $y = f(x)g(x)$. What is its y-intercept?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine and simplify an equation for $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify any holes and asymptotes and state the domain and range of $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$. Give the y-coordinate of the hole.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** Factor $g$: $g(x) = (x + {{a}})(x + {{b}})$, so
$y = f(x)g(x) = (x + {{a}})^2(x + {{b}})$.
Expanded: $y = x^3 + {{2*a+b}}x^2 + {{a*a+2*a*b}}x + {{a*a*b}}$.

**(b)** Zeros: $x = -{{a}}$ (order 2, graph touches and turns) and $x = -{{b}}$ (order 1, graph crosses). y-intercept: ${{a*a*b}}$. Cubic with positive leading coefficient: falls to the left, rises to the right. Domain and range: $\mathbb{R}$.

**(c)** $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{x + {{a}}}{(x + {{a}})(x + {{b}})} = \dfrac{1}{x + {{b}}}$, $x \ne -{{a}}, -{{b}}$.

**(d)** Hole where the factor cancels: $x = -{{a}}$, $y = \dfrac{1}{ -{{a}} + {{b}} } = {{1/(b-a):3}}$, so the hole is at $(-{{a}}, {{1/(b-a):3}})$.
Vertical asymptote $x = -{{b}}$; horizontal asymptote $y = 0$.
Domain $\{x \in \mathbb{R}, x \ne -{{a}}, -{{b}}\}$; range $\{y \in \mathbb{R}, y \ne 0, y \ne {{1/(b-a):3}}\}$.

rubric.point: Factors g(x) correctly
Correct product in factored and expanded form
Correct zeros with orders, y-intercept and end behaviour
Correct simplified quotient with both restrictions
Correct hole coordinates
Correct asymptotes, domain and range

parts.label: a
parts.text: For which values of $x$ is $y = \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ undefined? Explain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Simplify $\dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)}$, stating restrictions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens on the graph at each excluded value. Give the y-coordinate of any hole.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $v(x) = (x - {{a}})(x + {{a}}) = 0$ when $x = \pm {{a}}$. So $y = \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ is undefined for $x = {{a}}$ and $x = -{{a}}$.

**(b)** $\dfrac{x - {{a}}}{(x - {{a}})(x + {{a}})} = \dfrac{1}{x + {{a}}}$, $x \ne \pm{{a}}$.

**(c)** At $x = {{a}}$ the factor cancels → hole at $\left({{a}}, \dfrac{1}{ {{2*a}} }\right) = ({{a}}, {{1/(2*a):3}})$. At $x = -{{a}}$ the factor remains → vertical asymptote. Horizontal asymptote $y = 0$.

rubric.point: Identifies both excluded values ±a
Correct simplified form with restrictions
Identifies the hole and its coordinates
Identifies the vertical and horizontal asymptotes

questions.text: Without graphing, classify each function as even, odd or neither. Justify each answer using the symmetry of its factors, then prove one of them algebraically.\n\n(i) $y = x^2\cos x$  (ii) $y = x\sin x$  (iii) $y = x^3\cos x$  (iv) $y = \dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}$  (v) $y = x^2 + \sin x$
questions.modelAnswer:
(i) even × even = **even**.
(ii) odd × odd = **even**.
(iii) odd × even = **odd**.
(iv) odd ÷ even = **odd** (domain $x \ne 0$, which is symmetric).
(v) This is a **sum** of an even and an odd function, so the product rule does not apply: $h(-x) = x^2 - \sin x$, which is neither $h(x)$ nor $-h(x)$ → **neither**.

Proof of (iii): $h(-x) = (-x)^3\cos(-x) = -x^3\cos x = -h(x)$, so $h$ is odd.

rubric.point: Correct classification of (i) and (ii)
Correct classification of (iii) and (iv)
Recognizes that (v) is a sum and is neither, with justification
Correct algebraic proof using f(−x)

questions.text: Let $f$ be an even function and $g$ an odd function, both defined for all real numbers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that $y = f(x)g(x)$ is odd.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove that $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ is odd where it is defined.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ must always be undefined at $x = 0$. Illustrate with an example.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $h(x) = f(x)g(x)$: $h(-x) = f(-x)g(-x) = f(x)[-g(x)] = -h(x)$ → odd.

**(b)** $k(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ (where $g(x) \ne 0$): $k(-x) = \dfrac{f(-x)}{g(-x)} = \dfrac{f(x)}{-g(x)} = -k(x)$ → odd.

**(c)** Example: $f(x) = \cos x$, $g(x) = x$. $\dfrac{\cos x}{x}$ is odd; it is undefined at $x = 0$ because $g(0) = 0$ – every odd function defined at 0 has $g(0) = -g(0)$, so $g(0) = 0$. Hence an odd denominator always creates a restriction (often a vertical asymptote) at $x = 0$.

rubric.point: Correct proof that even × odd is odd
Correct proof that even ÷ odd is odd
Explains why an odd denominator causes a restriction at x = 0, with example

questions.text: A baseball team reduces ticket prices according to $P(g) = {{p0}} - 0.1g$ dollars, where $g$ is the number of games played. Attendance, in hundreds, is modelled by $N(g) = {{n0}} + 0.2g$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Develop an algebraic model for $R(g) = P(g)N(g)$ and explain what it represents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After how many games is revenue a maximum, and what is the maximum revenue?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Will the owners increase or decrease their ticket revenue under this plan? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $R(g) = P(g)N(g) = ({{p0}} - 0.1g)({{n0}} + 0.2g)$
$= {{p0*n0}} + {{0.2*p0}}g - {{0.1*n0}}g - 0.02g^2 = -0.02g^2 + {{0.2*p0-0.1*n0:3}}g + {{p0*n0}}$.
$R$ is revenue from ticket sales in hundreds of dollars.

**(b)** Vertex: $g = -\dfrac{ {{0.2*p0-0.1*n0:3}} }{2(-0.02)} = {{(0.2*p0-0.1*n0)/0.04:3}}$.
$R_{max} = ({{p0}} - 0.1({{(0.2*p0-0.1*n0)/0.04:3}}))({{n0}} + 0.2({{(0.2*p0-0.1*n0)/0.04:3}})) \approx {{(p0-0.1*(0.2*p0-0.1*n0)/0.04)*(n0+0.2*(0.2*p0-0.1*n0)/0.04):4}}$ hundred dollars.

**(c)** Revenue increases until about game {{(0.2*p0-0.1*n0)/0.04:3}} and then decreases, so the plan raises revenue in the short term but eventually the falling price outweighs the extra fans. Only $g \ge 0$ (and $P > 0$) has meaning.

rubric.point: Correct product and expansion of the revenue function
Interprets R(g) as revenue in hundreds of dollars
Correct game number of maximum revenue
Correct maximum revenue
Interprets the trend and restricts the domain

questions.text: At a team's games, the number of free caps given away (hundreds) is $C(g) = {{c0}} - 0.04g$, and attendance (hundreds) is $N(g) = 10 + 0.2g$, where $g$ is the game number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Develop a model for $p(g) = \dfrac{C(g)}{N(g)}$ and explain what it represents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the probability of receiving a cap at game {{k}}?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend of $p(g)$. At what game does it reach zero?

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $p(g) = \dfrac{C(g)}{N(g)} = \dfrac{ {{c0}} - 0.04g }{10 + 0.2g}$. It is caps ÷ fans, i.e. the probability that a randomly chosen fan receives a cap.

**(b)** $p({{k}}) = \dfrac{ {{c0}} - 0.04({{k}}) }{10 + 0.2({{k}})} = \dfrac{ {{c0-0.04*k:3}} }{ {{10+0.2*k:3}} } \approx {{(c0-0.04*k)/(10+0.2*k):2}}$, about {{100*(c0-0.04*k)/(10+0.2*k):2}}%.

**(c)** Numerator decreases and denominator increases, so $p(g)$ decreases; it reaches 0 when $C(g) = 0$: $g = {{c0/0.04:3}}$. After that no caps are given away.

rubric.point: Correct quotient model and interpretation as a probability
Correct probability at game k
Explains the decreasing trend
Finds when the probability becomes zero

questions.text: A fish pond starts with {{P0}} fish. With enough food the population grows as $P(t) = {{P0}}(1.05)^t$ ($t$ in years). The food supply, in units (1 unit feeds 1 fish for 1 year), is $F(t) = {{F0}}(0.92)^t$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the nature of $P(t)$ and $F(t)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the time of the crisis point, when the population equals the number of food units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine and interpret $y = \dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)}$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the living conditions of the fish before, at and after the crisis point. Comment on the validity of the model for $P(t)$ after the crisis point.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $P$ is exponential growth (base 1.05 > 1); $F$ is exponential decay (base 0.92 < 1).

**(b)** The crisis point is where $P(t) = F(t)$:
${{P0}}(1.05)^t = {{F0}}(0.92)^t \Rightarrow \left(\dfrac{1.05}{0.92}\right)^t = \dfrac{ {{F0}} }{ {{P0}} }$
$t = \dfrac{\log({{F0}}/{{P0}})}{\log(1.05/0.92)} \approx {{log(F0/P0)/log(1.05/0.92):3}}$ years.
Then $P \approx {{P0*1.05^(log(F0/P0)/log(1.05/0.92)):3}}$ fish (= food units).

**(c)** $y = \dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)} = \dfrac{ {{F0}} }{ {{P0}} }\left(\dfrac{0.92}{1.05}\right)^t$ is food per fish – an exponential decay function. It equals 1 at the crisis point.

**(d)** Before the crisis point $F/P > 1$: more than enough food. At it, exactly enough. After it, $F/P < 1$: a shortage – the model $P(t) = {{P0}}(1.05)^t$ is no longer valid, because the population would level off or decline.

rubric.point: Describes both functions correctly
Sets up P(t) = F(t) correctly
Solves for the crisis time using logarithms
Correct quotient function and interpretation
Explains conditions before/at/after and validity of the model

questions.text: The population of a country is $P(t) = 6(1.02)^t$ million, $t$ years after 2000. Food production can sustain $F(t) = 8 + 0.04t$ million people for one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend of each function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does $y = F(t) - P(t)$ represent? Is there a surplus or a shortage in 2000?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the food production per capita, $\dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)}$, at $t = {{k}}$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what $\dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)} > 1$ and $\dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)} < 1$ mean, and predict the long-term situation.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $P$ grows exponentially (2% per year); $F$ grows linearly (0.04 million per year).

**(b)** $y = F(t) - P(t)$ is the food surplus (positive) or shortage (negative), in millions of people fed. At $t = 0$: $8 - 6 = 2$, a surplus.

**(c)** Food per capita $= \dfrac{F(t)}{P(t)}$. At $t = {{k}}$: $\dfrac{8 + 0.04({{k}})}{6(1.02)^{ {{k}} }} \approx \dfrac{ {{8+0.04*k:4}} }{ {{6*1.02^k:4}} } \approx {{(8+0.04*k)/(6*1.02^k):3}}$.

**(d)** $\dfrac{F}{P} > 1$ means a surplus, $< 1$ a shortage. Because exponential growth eventually outpaces linear growth, $F/P$ decreases and drops below 1 (around $t \approx 16$, i.e. 2016, by graphing). Long-term, the country must increase food production or imports.

rubric.point: Describes the growth types
Interprets F − P and its initial value
Correct per-capita value at t = k
Explains the meaning of F/P > 1 and < 1
Uses exponential vs linear growth to predict a long-term shortage

questions.text: A pendulum's horizontal displacement is $x(t) = {{A}}\cos({{k}}t)({{b}})^t$, in centimetres, $t$ in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At what horizontal distance from rest was the pendulum released?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which component causes the periodic motion and which causes the decay? Find the period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After what time has the amplitude diminished to 50% of its initial value?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the amplitude after {{T}} s.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Name the type of motion and state the domain and range in context.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $x(0) = {{A}}\cos 0 \cdot {{b}}^0 = {{A}}$ cm.

**(b)** $\cos({{k}}t)$ produces the periodic motion; period $= \dfrac{2\pi}{ {{k}} } \approx {{2*pi/k:3}}$ s. The factor $({{b}})^t$ makes the amplitude decay.

**(c)** Amplitude $= {{A}}({{b}})^t$. Half: $({{b}})^t = 0.5 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\log 0.5}{\log {{b}}} \approx {{log(0.5)/log(b):3}}$ s.

**(d)** At $t = {{T}}$ s the amplitude is ${{A}}({{b}})^{ {{T}} } \approx {{A*b^T:3}}$ cm.

**(e)** The motion is damped harmonic motion; domain $t \ge 0$, range $-{{A}} \le x \le {{A}}$.

rubric.point: Correct release displacement

questions.text: The motion of a child on a swing after a single push can be modelled by $y(t) = A\sin(kt)\cdot c^t$, where $A$, $k$ and $c$ are constants with $0 < c < 1$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What two component functions are combined? Describe each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the combined function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How would the constants change if air resistance were reduced, or if the swing's chains were longer? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** A sinusoidal function $A\sin(kt)$ (periodic, constant amplitude) and an exponential decay $c^t$ (decreasing, always positive).

**(b)** The graph oscillates between the envelope curves $y = Ac^t$ and $y = -Ac^t$, crossing the t-axis wherever $\sin(kt) = 0$, with amplitude shrinking toward 0.

**(c)** Less air resistance → slower decay → $c$ closer to 1 (envelope flatter). A longer swing (pendulum) → longer period → smaller $k$ (oscillations more spread out). A bigger push → larger $A$.

rubric.point: Identifies both component functions and their shapes
Describes the combined graph and its envelope
Correctly links physical changes to changes in c, k and A

parts.label: a
parts.text: Develop an algebraic model for $y = f(x)g(x)$ and give its domain and range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, its domain, and any holes or asymptotes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine $y = \dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)}$, its domain, and any holes or asymptotes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate both quotients at $x = {{k}}$ and comment.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $y = f(x)g(x) = x^3 + {{c}}x^2 + {{d}}x + {{c*d}}$. Cubic: domain and range $\mathbb{R}$; one real zero $x = -{{c}}$ (since $x^2 + {{d}} > 0$).

**(b)** $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{x + {{c}}}{x^2 + {{d}}}$. The denominator is never zero, so the domain is $\mathbb{R}$; there are no vertical asymptotes or holes. Horizontal asymptote $y = 0$ (degree of denominator is larger).

**(c)** $y = \dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)} = \dfrac{x^2 + {{d}}}{x + {{c}}}$: domain $x \ne -{{c}}$, vertical asymptote $x = -{{c}}$ (numerator is not zero there), no hole.

**(d)** $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)({{k}}) = \dfrac{ {{k+c}} }{ {{k*k+d}} } \approx {{(k+c)/(k*k+d):3}}$ and $\left(\dfrac{g}{f}\right)({{k}}) \approx {{(k*k+d)/(k+c):3}}$ – reciprocals of each other.

rubric.point: Correct product with domain and range
Correct domain of f/g with reason (no zeros of g)
Identifies the horizontal asymptote of f/g
Correct domain and vertical asymptote of g/f
Correct values and the observation that they are reciprocals

questions.text: Let $u(x) = \cos x$ and $v(x) = ({{b}})^x$. Work in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe $y = u(x)v(x)$ and evaluate it at $x = \pi$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe $y = \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ and give its domain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give the domain of $y = \dfrac{v(x)}{u(x)}$ and identify any asymptotes.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $y = u(x)v(x) = ({{b}})^x\cos x$: oscillates with amplitude $({{b}})^x$; domain $\mathbb{R}$. Since $0 < {{b}} < 1$, the amplitude decays as $x$ increases and grows as $x$ decreases – damped oscillation. $(uv)(\pi) = ({{b}})^{\pi}\cos\pi \approx {{-b^pi:3}}$.

**(b)** $y = \dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} = \dfrac{\cos x}{ ({{b}})^x }$: $v(x) > 0$ always, so domain $\mathbb{R}$, no asymptotes; its amplitude **grows** as $x$ increases.

**(c)** $y = \dfrac{v(x)}{u(x)} = \dfrac{ ({{b}})^x }{\cos x}$: undefined where $\cos x = 0$, i.e. $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ → vertical asymptotes there. Domain $\{x \in \mathbb{R}, x \ne \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\}$.

rubric.point: Correct description and value of the product
Correct domain/behaviour of u/v
Identifies the vertical asymptotes of v/u with general form
Correct domain of v/u

questions.text: After a school dance, the probability that Carlos asks Keiko on a date $t$ days later is $p_A(t) = 0.45\sin t + 0.5$. The probability that Keiko says yes, if asked, is $p_Y(t) = -0.08t(t - 7)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend of each function, the domain in context, and the maximum of $p_Y(t)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When is Carlos most likely to ask, to the nearest tenth of a day?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the probability that they agree to a date is $y = p_A(t)p_Y(t)$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate this probability at $t = {{k}}$.

parts.label: e
parts.text: When does Carlos have no chance? What advice would you give him?

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $p_A$ oscillates between 0.05 and 0.95 (period $2\pi$). $p_Y$ is a downward parabola, $\ge 0$ only for $0 \le t \le 7$, so the context domain is $[0, 7]$. Max of $p_Y$ at $t = 3.5$: $p_Y(3.5) = -0.08(3.5)(-3.5) = 0.98$.

**(b)** $p_A$ is greatest when $\sin t = 1$: $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.6$ days.

**(c)** The probability that they agree on a date is the product $y = p_A(t)\,p_Y(t)$ (Carlos asks **and** Keiko says yes).

**(d)** $y({{k}}) = (0.45\sin {{k}} + 0.5)(-0.08)({{k}})({{k}} - 7) \approx ({{0.45*sin(k)+0.5:3}})({{-0.08*k*(k-7):3}}) \approx {{(0.45*sin(k)+0.5)*(-0.08*k*(k-7)):2}}$.

**(e)** At $t = 0$ and $t = 7$, $p_Y = 0$, so the product is 0 – after 7 days Carlos has no chance. Advice: ask soon – between about day 1.5 and day 3 the product is largest.

rubric.point: Describes both functions and the context domain
Finds when Carlos is most likely to ask
Explains why the joint probability is a product
Correct value of the product at t = k
Identifies zero-probability times and gives reasoned advice

questions.text: A mathematical operation is **commutative** if reversing the order of the operands gives the same result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Is the product of functions commutative? Use an example and explain why.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Is the quotient of functions commutative? Use an example to support your answer.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** Yes. Example $f(x) = x^2$, $g(x) = \sin x$: $f(x)g(x) = x^2\sin x = (\sin x)x^2 = g(x)f(x)$. In general, at every $x$ we multiply two real numbers, and multiplication of real numbers is commutative.

**(b)** No. $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{x^2}{\sin x}$ but $\dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)} = \dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}$; at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ these are $\frac{\pi^2}{4} \approx 2.47$ and $\frac{4}{\pi^2} \approx 0.405$. The two quotients are **reciprocals**; they also have different domains (zeros of $\sin x$ vs. $x = 0$).

rubric.point: States products are commutative with example and reason
States quotients are not commutative with a numerical counterexample
Notes the quotients are reciprocals / have different domains

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate $(fg)(1)$.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $f$: upper semicircle of radius {{r}}, domain $[-{{r}}, {{r}}]$, **even** ($f(-x) = f(x)$). $g$: odd.

**(b)** $y = f(x)g(x) = \sqrt{ {{r*r}} - x^2}\,\sin x$ is even × odd = **odd**. Domain: common domain $[-{{r}}, {{r}}]$.

**(c)** $y = \dfrac{g(x)}{f(x)} = \dfrac{\sin x}{\sqrt{ {{r*r}} - x^2}}$: odd ÷ even = odd. Denominator is 0 at $x = \pm{{r}}$, so the domain is $(-{{r}}, {{r}})$, with vertical asymptotes at $x = \pm {{r}}$ (since $\sin {{r}} \ne 0$).

**(d)** $(fg)(1) = \sqrt{ {{r*r-1}} }\sin 1 \approx {{sqrt(r*r-1)*sin(1):3}}$.

rubric.point: Identifies the shape, domain and symmetry of f
Classifies the product as odd and gives its domain
Correct domain and asymptotes of g/f with reasons
Correct value of (fg)(1)

questions.text: Create your own combined functions that meet given conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write two functions, one even and one odd, whose product is odd. Verify algebraically.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ so that $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = 2$ and a hole at $x = -1$. Give the coordinates of the hole.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a product function that models an oscillation that starts at 5 units, has period 2 s and slowly loses amplitude. Explain your choices.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** Example: $f(x) = x$ (odd), $g(x) = x^2 + 1$ (even). $y = f(x)g(x) = x^3 + x$ is odd. ✓ (Any odd × even pair works.)

**(b)** Need the denominator zero at $x = 2$ but not the numerator: $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2}$ → VA $x = 2$; and a hole at $x = -1$ needs a common factor: $\dfrac{(x+1)(x+3)}{(x+1)(x-2)}$ = $\dfrac{x+3}{x-2}$, $x \ne -1$: hole at $(-1, -\tfrac23)$, VA $x = 2$. So $f(x) = (x+1)(x+3)$, $g(x) = (x+1)(x-2)$.

**(c)** A damped wave: $y = 5\cos(\pi t)(0.8)^t$ – amplitude 5 at $t = 0$, period 2, decaying. Justification: cosine starts at its maximum; base 0.8 < 1 gives decay.

rubric.point: Valid odd product with justification
Valid quotient with the required asymptote and hole, verified
Valid damped oscillation meeting the conditions, justified

questions.text: Let $f(x)$ be an even function and $g(x)$ an odd function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the symmetry of $[f(x)]^n$ for any positive integer $n$? Prove it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the symmetry of $[g(x)]^n$? Explain how it depends on $n$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Illustrate (b) with $g(x) = \sin x$ for $n = 2$ and $n = 3$.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $[f(x)]^2$, $[f(x)]^3$, … $[f(x)]^n$ are all **even**: $[f(-x)]^n = [f(x)]^n$.

**(b)** $[g(-x)]^n = [-g(x)]^n = (-1)^n[g(x)]^n$: even when $n$ is even, odd when $n$ is odd. Example: $\sin^2 x$ is even (period $\pi$), $\sin^3 x$ is odd.

**(c)** $y = \sin^2 x$ is even and its range is $[0, 1]$; $y = \sin^3 x$ is odd with range $[-1, 1]$.

rubric.point: Correct result and proof for powers of an even function
Correct result and proof for powers of an odd function, depending on n
Correct examples with symmetry
